```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3)
```

This vignette uses comdynamite, which implements the model of Thompson et al.
(2020), to ask an ecological question: **how do dispersal,
phylogenetic signal in niches and competition among relatives combine to shape
the phylogenetic structure of local communities?** Phylogenetic clustering is
often read as evidence of environmental filtering on conserved niches, and
overdispersion as evidence of competition (Webb et al. 2002). Because a
simulation fixes the processes, it shows how far those readings hold once
dispersal also operates.

The simulations take a few minutes, so the results were computed in advance and
are loaded below. The complete script is
[`data-raw/vignette_ecology.R`](https://github.com/diogoprov/comdynamite/blob/main/data-raw/vignette_ecology.R).

## Design

We cross three factors:

* **dispersal**, the emigration probability, from 0.001 to 0.5;
* **niche conservatism**: optima without phylogenetic signal (`lambda = 0`) or
  evolving under Brownian motion (`lambda = 1`);
* **competition**: none among species, or stronger between close relatives.

Each replicate draws one tree of 30 species and one landscape of 25 sites, and
uses them in all scenarios, so that scenarios are compared on the same regional
pool. Traits are drawn once per value of `lambda` and shared across dispersal
rates and competition types.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(comdynamite)

tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(30)
land <- landscape_implicit(25)
traits <- species_traits(tree, lambda = 1, sigma_mean = 8, sigma_sd = 2)
alpha <- competition_matrix(tree, "phylo", inter_max = 0.5)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(land, traits, alpha, dispersal = 0.01, n_steps = 1000)
```

For each simulation we record the mean local richness (alpha), the number of
species in the metacommunity (gamma), the mean pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity
among sites (beta), and the standardised effect size of the mean pairwise
distance (SES MPD; computed with picante, Kembel et al. 2010), averaged over
sites. SES MPD is negative under phylogenetic
clustering and positive under overdispersion.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pa <- (sim$abundance > 0) * 1
pa <- pa[rowSums(pa) > 1, , drop = FALSE]
z <- picante::ses.mpd(pa, cophenetic(tree), null.model = "taxa.labels",
                      runs = 99)$mpd.obs.z
mean(z[is.finite(z)])
```

`run_scenarios()` runs the whole design: `setup` draws what a replicate shares, and
`summary_stats()` gives alpha, gamma, SES MPD and others, with beta as gamma / alpha.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
scenarios <- expand.grid(dispersal = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5), lambda = c(0, 1),
                         competition = c("none", "phylo"))
pool <- function() {
  list(tree = treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(30), landscape = landscape_implicit(25))
}
one_run <- function(scenario, shared) {
  simulate_metacommunity(shared$landscape,
                         species_traits(shared$tree, scenario$lambda, sigma_mean = 8, sigma_sd = 2),
                         competition_matrix(shared$tree, as.character(scenario$competition),
                                            inter_max = 0.5),
                         dispersal = scenario$dispersal, n_steps = 1000)
}
results <- run_scenarios(scenarios, one_run, pool, n_rep = 20)
```

Here traits are drawn in each scenario. To share them across dispersal rates and competition
types, as we did, draw them in `setup`.

The null model draws from all the species in the tree, which is the regional
pool. Using only the species that persisted would remove the effect of regional
extinction from the comparison.

## Results

```{r}
results <- readRDS("phylogenetic-structure.rds")
means <- aggregate(cbind(alpha, gamma, beta, ses_mpd) ~ dispersal + lambda + competition,
                   data = results, FUN = mean)
knitr::kable(means, digits = 2)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.2, fig.alt = "SES MPD, local richness and beta diversity against dispersal, for the four combinations of phylogenetic signal and competition."}
groups <- unique(means[c("lambda", "competition")])
cols <- c("#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#D55E00")
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0))
for (v in c("ses_mpd", "alpha", "beta")) {
  plot(means$dispersal, means[[v]], log = "x", type = "n", xlab = "dispersal",
       ylab = c(ses_mpd = "SES MPD", alpha = "local richness", beta = "beta (Jaccard)")[v])
  if (v == "ses_mpd") abline(h = 0, col = "grey70")
  for (g in seq_len(nrow(groups))) {
    d <- means[means$lambda == groups$lambda[g] &
                 means$competition == groups$competition[g], ]
    lines(d$dispersal, d[[v]], col = cols[g], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 15 + g)
  }
}
legend("bottomleft", paste0("lambda = ", groups$lambda, ", ", groups$competition),
       col = cols, pch = 15 + seq_len(nrow(groups)), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(old)
```

Four patterns stand out.

**Clustering needs both conserved niches and limited dispersal.** Without
competition and with `lambda = 1`, communities are clustered at low dispersal
(SES MPD near -1.3) and the signal weakens as dispersal increases, to between
-0.3 and -0.5 at the highest rates. Niche conservatism alone does not produce clustering: immigrants keep
species in sites that do not suit them, so composition no longer reflects the
match between niches and environment.

**Without phylogenetic signal, filtering leaves no phylogenetic trace.** With
`lambda = 0` and no competition, SES MPD stays near zero at all dispersal rates,
even though species are strongly sorted by the environment at low dispersal
(beta near 0.8).

**Competition among relatives can hide filtering.** With `lambda = 1`,
competition among relatives moves SES MPD from about -1.3 to about zero at the
lowest dispersal rate, which is close to the random expectation although both
processes are acting strongly. At higher dispersal, communities become
slightly overdispersed. A value near zero therefore does not imply that assembly is
random.

**Taxonomic beta diversity does not see the phylogenetic signal.** Beta diversity
depends on dispersal and competition but is the same for `lambda = 0` and
`lambda = 1`. In this model, the signal changes which relatives co-occur, not how
different sites are in composition.

Competition also reduces the size of the metacommunity: it halves local richness
and, at the highest dispersal rate, gamma falls to about 11 of the 30 species.
A likely explanation, which these simulations do not test directly, is that high
dispersal exposes all species to the same competitors in every site.

## Limitations

These results hold for the values used here. They come from one tree size, one
landscape size and one strength of competition, and the magnitudes will change
with those choices. The means are also averages over 30 replicates with a
standard error of up to 0.2 for SES MPD, so small differences between scenarios
should not be interpreted.

With competition among relatives and high dispersal, 1000 steps is not an
equilibrium: in a test run, regional exclusion continued slowly up to 3000 steps.
Without competition, richness was stable by 300 steps. Before drawing conclusions
from a new parameter set, check that the statistics of interest have stabilised,
for example with `record_steps` in `simulate_metacommunity()`.

SES MPD here uses presence and absence, so a single immigrant counts as much as
a large population. Sink populations therefore have their full weight, and an
abundance-weighted statistic may show a weaker effect of dispersal.
